title: Buying fruit at a market in Mexico City
setting: It's Saturday morning at a market in Coyoacán, Mexico City. Stalls are piled high with mangoes, papayas and limes, and vendors are calling out to people walking by. You stop at Doña Lupe's fruit stall.
objectives: Ask how much something costs per kilo
Buy a specific amount, like half a kilo
Finish the purchase politely and pay
varietyNote: These expressions are common in Mexico City and much of central Mexico. Market talk varies across Mexico and Latin America, and "¿Cuánto cuesta…?" is understood everywhere Spanish is spoken.

phrases.exampleTranslation: How much is a kilo of mangoes?
phrases.note: A very common way to ask prices at Mexican markets. "¿A cómo está…?" is also heard.

phrases.example: El mango está a cuarenta el kilo.
phrases.exampleTranslation: Mangoes are forty pesos a kilo.

phrases.translation: Give me half a kilo, please.
phrases.example: Deme medio kilo de limones, por favor.
phrases.exampleTranslation: Half a kilo of limes, please.
phrases.note: "Deme" uses "usted", the polite form that's common with market vendors in Mexico. You'll also hear "un cuarto" (a quarter kilo).
Fruit vendors often offer a taste before you buy.

phrases.example: Perdón, solo traigo un billete de quinientos. ¿Tiene cambio?
phrases.exampleTranslation: Sorry, I only have a 500 note. Do you have change?

cultureNotes: Vendors call out "¡Pásele, pásele!" (Come on in!) and use friendly forms of address like "marchante" (customer), "joven" or "güero/güera". It's sales talk, used very loosely with customers.
"Usted" is common when talking to vendors and older people. For "you" plural, Latin America uses "ustedes" — "vosotros" isn't used.
Many stalls are cash only, and small notes and coins are appreciated. Paying for a few pesos of fruit with a 500-peso note can be a problem.
Prices at food stalls are usually fixed. Bargaining is more common for crafts ("artesanías") than for fruit and vegetables.

steps.text: As you walk up, Doña Lupe is calling out to a woman passing by: "¡Pásele, güerita!" Then she turns to you.

steps.speaker: Doña Lupe
steps.translation: Come on in! What can we get you?

steps.prompt: Doña Lupe called the woman passing by "güerita". What does it usually mean here?

options.text: It's friendly sales talk — vendors use it loosely with all kinds of customers.
options.why: Right. Literally it relates to fair hair or skin, but at a market it's mostly just a warm way to address customers. You'll also hear "güero", "joven" and "marchante" (customer) — like she called you.
Not at all — it's meant to be friendly and welcoming.

options.text: She thinks she knows you from somewhere.
options.why: Vendors say this to passers-by all the time. It's just a friendly way to get someone's attention.

steps.prompt: The mangoes look great. How do you ask the price per kilo, market-style?

options.why: This is how prices are typically asked at Mexican markets. "¿Cuánto cuesta el kilo?" works too.
This asks how many mangoes are in a kilo, not how much it costs.
A mix-up with "¿Cómo estás?" (How are you?). For the price, ask about the kilo: "¿A cómo el kilo?"

steps.speaker: Doña Lupe
steps.text: Está a cuarenta el kilo, marchante. ¿Le doy a probar?
steps.translation: It's forty a kilo. Would you like a taste?

options.text: It's 40 pesos a kilo, and she's offering you a taste.
options.why: "Está a cuarenta" = it's (selling) at forty; "¿Le doy a probar?" = shall I give you a taste?

options.text: There are 40 mangoes in a kilo, and she's asking if you want to buy them.
options.why: "Está a cuarenta el kilo" is about the price, not the number of mangoes.

options.text: It's 14 pesos a kilo, and she's asking if you'd like to try a different fruit.
options.why: Fourteen is "catorce" — "cuarenta" is forty. And "probar" is about tasting this fruit.

steps.text: You try a slice. It's delicious.

steps.prompt: You'd like half a kilo. What do you say?

options.why: Clear and polite. "Medio kilo" is how half a kilo is said.

options.text: Deme un kilo y medio, por favor.
options.why: That's one and a half kilos — three times what you wanted!

options.text: Quiero la mitad de un kilo.
options.why: You'd be understood, but it sounds clunky and a little blunt. "Medio kilo, por favor" is the natural way.

steps.prompt: That's all you need. How do you answer?

options.why: A very common, polite way to say "That's everything" in Mexico. "Es todo, gracias" works too.
This means "I've finished", as if you'd finished eating or a task, not shopping.
Understood, but it sounds like you're refusing something you didn't like. "Sería todo, gracias" is friendlier.

steps.prompt: You only have a 500-peso note. What's the best thing to do?

options.text: Apologise and ask "¿Tiene cambio?" — and try to carry smaller notes and coins next time.
options.why: Right. Small stalls often can't change big notes, so asking first is polite.

options.text: Hand it over — market vendors always have plenty of change.
options.why: Small stalls often don't, especially early in the day. A 500 note for 20 pesos can leave them short.

options.text: Ask to pay by card instead.
options.why: Some stalls take cards or transfers now, but many are cash only. Ask rather than assume.

steps.speaker: Doña Lupe
steps.text: No se preocupe, aquí tiene su cambio. ¡Que le vaya bien!
steps.translation: Don't worry, here's your change. Have a good day!
